utterances.text: And Josh Elliott, who's an Al Van Fellow.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: And then just finally, I want to say, I know we've probably mentioned it in the past, but the loss of Gloria Steinem is a big deal for many of us.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: Her service is going to be in the middle of November, and if anybody wants to attend, it's an invitation only.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: Let me know.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: David M. Carr
utterances.text: Thank you, Councilman Brewer.

utterances.speaker: David M. Carr
utterances.text: Councilman Murano, followed by Councilman Brooks-Powers.

chapters.summary: Morano introduces Intro 1117, requiring developers converting properties to transient hotels to prepare a community impact statement on traffic, emergency response, infrastructure, and neighborhood fit before permits are issued.
chapters.title: Council Member Morano Introduces Intro 1117 on Community Impact Statements for Transient Hotels

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: Thank you, Majority Leader at Interim.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: Colleagues, today I'm introducing Intro 1117, a bill based on a pretty radical idea.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: Before you build something that could significantly affect the neighborhood, you ought to tell the neighborhood what the impact will be.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: I know.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: Revolutionary stuff.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: This legislation was inspired by a proposed 160-bed homeless shelter in Miami.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: district on Arthur Kill Road, filed with the Department of Buildings as a transient hotel.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: Now, colleagues, we can disagree about where shelters belong, we can disagree about how best to address homelessness, but surely we can agree that communities deserve basic information before major projects move forward.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: What's the impact on traffic?

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: What's the impact on police and fire response, on our sewers, on our infrastructure?

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: Does the project fit the surrounding neighborhood?

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: These aren't trick questions.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: They're the kinds of questions any responsible government should be asking.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: So my bill would require developers building or converting properties into transient hotels to prepare a community impact statement addressing those concerns.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: It would be shared with the local elected officials and community boards and made available to the public before permits are issued.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: Simple as that.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: Let me be clear.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: This is not a bill to stop homeless shelters.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: It's a bill to stop government from keeping communities in the dark about what's happening in their own neighborhood.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: It doesn't give anybody a veto.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: It doesn't require unanimous neighborhood approval.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: Frankly, if we required unanimous agreement on anything in New York City, we'd still be debating where to put the Brooklyn Bridge.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: It simply says that transparency should come before the decision, not after.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: Whether you represent Staten Island, the Bronx, Brooklyn, Queens, or Manhattan, your constituents deserve the same respect.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: And I hope my colleagues will join me in supporting this common sense legislation.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: David M. Carr
utterances.text: Thank you, Councilman Rano.

utterances.speaker: David M. Carr
utterances.text: Councilman Brooks-Powers, followed by Councilman Epstein.

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: Thank you.

chapters.summary: Brooks-Powers introduces Intro 1104, requiring the Department of Probation to provide written notice and explain rights before intake interviews for youth accused of crimes.
chapters.title: Council Member Brooks-Powers Introduces Intro 1104 on Youth Rights in Probation Intake

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: I am proud to introduce two bills today concerning the Department of Probation.

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: The first, Intro 1104, would give youth accused of crimes clear information about the criminal legal process after a young person is arrested for an offense which can be heard in family court.

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: They and their family will often meet with the Department of Probation.

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: For an intake interview that can determine whether the case is resolved without court via adjustment or continues through the court system.

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: Because an attorney is generally not present during that intake interview, families frequently navigate this moment without counsel and may share information or sign paperwork without knowing the consequences.

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: This bill would require the department to provide a written notice before intake explaining the process and identifying organizations that provide legal representation to youth.

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: At the start of the interview, the department would also inform the youth and their family of their rights, including

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: how the information they share may be used and what signing any paperwork entails.

chapters.summary: Brooks-Powers introduces Intro 1103, recognizing probation officers as uniformed officers for collective bargaining to address pay and working condition disparities.
chapters.title: Council Member Brooks-Powers Introduces Intro 1103 on Probation Officers as Uniformed

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: The second intro, 1103, concerns the officers who carry out the department's work.

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: Like our city's uniformed police, fire, Santa,

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: and correction officers, probation officers carry real public safety responsibilities.

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: Yet, under the city's collective bargaining law, they are not recognized among those uniformed forces and do not receive the same bargaining treatment.

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: This bill changes that, recognizing probation officers as uniformed officers for collective bargaining and helping to address a gap that has contributed to longstanding disparities in their pay

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: and working conditions, especially among female and non-white officers.

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: Together, these bills reflect a commitment to a probation system that is fair to the young people it serves and to the workforce it relies on.

chapters.summary: Brooks-Powers recognizes Lynette Townsley, Youth Subcommittee Chair of Community Board 12, and welcomes young people from Southeast Queens.
chapters.title: Council Member Brooks-Powers Recognizes Lynette Townsley and Youth

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: I invite my colleagues to join me in sponsoring these bills.

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: And lastly, I'd like to also recognize Lynette Townsley, the Youth Subcommittee Chair of Community Board 12, who had the pleasure of reorganizing the Jamaica branch of the NAACP Youth

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: Group, and all of the young people that joined today from Southeast Queens.

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: We welcome you in the People's House, and thank you.

utterances.speaker: David M. Carr
utterances.text: Thank you, Councilmember.

utterances.speaker: David M. Carr
utterances.text: Councilmember Epstein, followed by Councilmember Ressler.

chapters.summary: Epstein introduces Intro 1105, the Power Act, which creates a private right of action for consumer protection and expands protections for small businesses, tenants, homeowners, and workers against predatory practices.
chapters.title: Council Member Epstein Introduces Intro 1105, the Power Act

utterances.speaker: Harvey D. Epstein
utterances.text: Thank you, acting majority leaders.

utterances.speaker: Harvey D. Epstein
utterances.text: Good seeing you up there.

utterances.speaker: Harvey D. Epstein
utterances.text: Not many times, but today at least.

utterances.speaker: Harvey D. Epstein
utterances.text: I want to thank the speaker for introducing 1105 today.

utterances.speaker: Harvey D. Epstein
utterances.text: It's called the Power Act, along with the mayor and the commissioner of DCWP.

utterances.speaker: Harvey D. Epstein
utterances.text: The bill really changes some really fundamental things in consumer protection.

utterances.speaker: Harvey D. Epstein
utterances.text: One, it allows a private right of action.

utterances.speaker: Harvey D. Epstein
utterances.text: And two, the second component is it expands protections for small businesses across this great city.

utterances.speaker: Harvey D. Epstein
utterances.text: So in real life, some of the changes that we could see is tenants are being charged fees, let's say a $40 fee.

utterances.speaker: Harvey D. Epstein
utterances.text: They could be able to get that resolved through a legal services program.

utterances.speaker: Harvey D. Epstein
utterances.text: Homeowners, we talk about deed theft across the board.

utterances.speaker: Harvey D. Epstein
utterances.text: Homeowners would have real legal recourse with this if we changed the law.

utterances.speaker: Harvey D. Epstein
utterances.text: Small businesses see predatory financing time and time again that impacts their ability to stay alive.

utterances.speaker: Harvey D. Epstein
utterances.text: This change in the law could allow those small businesses to use the law to protect them.

utterances.speaker: Harvey D. Epstein
utterances.text: And worker exploitation.

utterances.speaker: Harvey D. Epstein
utterances.text: We see, just last week alone, the mayor announced, along with a lot of our colleagues, $130 million going back to low-wage workers.

utterances.speaker: Harvey D. Epstein
utterances.text: We could, in changing the law, allow workers across our great city to be able to do this.

utterances.speaker: Harvey D. Epstein
utterances.text: This would check corporate power.

utterances.speaker: Harvey D. Epstein
utterances.text: This would allow people to be able to fight back and give them real authority.

utterances.speaker: Harvey D. Epstein
utterances.text: I look forward to having you all look at this bill.

utterances.speaker: Harvey D. Epstein
utterances.text: I encourage you all to co-sponsor this.

utterances.speaker: Harvey D. Epstein
utterances.text: I want to thank leadership here, the Speaker and the Mayor, for bringing this issue forward.

utterances.speaker: Harvey D. Epstein
utterances.text: It's a fundamental change that exists in 43 states and the District of Columbia, and New York deserves to have it as well.

utterances.speaker: Harvey D. Epstein
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: David M. Carr
utterances.text: Thank you, Councilman Reftstein, for reminding me that I'm temporary.

utterances.speaker: David M. Carr
utterances.text: But you're all temporary.

utterances.speaker: David M. Carr
utterances.text: We're all temporary.

utterances.speaker: David M. Carr
utterances.text: So, you know.

utterances.speaker: David M. Carr
utterances.text: This is their fact.

utterances.speaker: David M. Carr
utterances.text: Councilmember Ressler, followed by Councilmember Nurse.

chapters.summary: Restler introduces a resolution defending Canada against hostile rhetoric from the White House, highlighting Canada as a major trading partner and source of tourism and culture for New York City.
chapters.title: Council Member Restler Introduces Resolution Defending Canada

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: Thank you so much to the briefly interim majority leader.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: I firstly just want to associate myself with the moving remarks by Councilmember Joseph.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: And I don't introduce very many resolutions, but I felt moved to...

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: Introduce a resolution defending Canada.

utterances.speaker: David M. Carr
utterances.text: I love you, Jim.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: My mom is from Montreal, and yeah, you could tell.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: It does.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: It adds up.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: But the White House's just stupidly hostile rhetoric toward Canada has made zero sense.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: Canada is among our city's largest trading partners.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: 12% of exports from New York City go to Canada.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: 16% of imports come from Canada.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: They are the second largest source of tourists into New York City.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: They have sent us many...

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: Very talented comedians and a couple good singers and and lots of great New Yorkers who are Canadian Americans

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: I think it's important as our cities as our nation's economic and cultural capital that we stand up and say that we respect our neighbors and we value

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: the relationship and that we condemn

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: just the needless hostility that the president has been displaying toward our friends up north.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: And I hope folks will sign on and that we can pass it.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: David M. Carr
utterances.text: Thank you, Council Member.

utterances.speaker: David M. Carr
utterances.text: Council Member Nurse?

chapters.summary: Nurse welcomes new fellow Leslie Gomez, a former intern, to the Council.
chapters.title: Council Member Nurse Welcomes New Fellow Leslie Gomez

utterances.speaker: Sandy Nurse
utterances.text: Thank you, Majority Leader.

utterances.speaker: Sandy Nurse
utterances.text: I just wanted to welcome our newest fellow, Leslie Gomez, to the council.

utterances.speaker: Sandy Nurse
utterances.text: We're really excited to work with her.

utterances.speaker: Sandy Nurse
utterances.text: She was an intern with our office a summer ago or two summers ago.

utterances.speaker: Sandy Nurse
utterances.text: I can't remember, but she was great.

utterances.speaker: Sandy Nurse
utterances.text: And we're super excited to have her back.

utterances.speaker: Sandy Nurse
utterances.text: Welcome back, Leslie.

utterances.speaker: Sandy Nurse
utterances.text: Thank you, Majority Leader.

chapters.summary: Majority Leader Carr concludes general discussion, Speaker Menin adjourns the stated meeting, and the gavel is banged.
chapters.title: Meeting Adjourned

utterances.speaker: David M. Carr
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: David M. Carr
utterances.text: That concludes general discussion.

utterances.speaker: David M. Carr
utterances.text: And now I'll call on Speaker Julie Menon to close today's stated meeting.

utterances.speaker: David M. Carr
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: David M. Carr
utterances.text: I don't want it to end, but, you know.

utterances.speaker: David M. Carr
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: At the stated meeting of October 8, 2026 is hereby adjourned.

utterances.speaker: David M. Carr

summary: The New York City Council held a stated meeting on October 8, 2026, featuring an invocation by Rabbi Yossi Mendelson, a roll call, and adoption of minutes.
The Council voted on land use call-ups and a general orders calendar including rezonings, tax exemptions, and several local laws on topics from AI oversight to towing databases.

Members delivered remarks and introduced new legislation on issues including AI safety, domestic violence reporting, food safety, and cultural recognitions, concluding with general discussion and adjournment.
